newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn, unswayed by doubters, says on course for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bonn, unswayed by doubters, says on course for EMU.

text.p: Bonn politicians on Thursday exuded confidence that Germany was on track to qualify for Europe's single currency, despite a report claiming that even the European Commission doubts Bonn's deficit forecast.

A further ray of optimism for Europe's largest economy came when independent economists predicted that an official growth target of 2.5 percent this year was still achievable, even though the pace of expansion was slow in the first quarter.
But two Bundesbank council members -- who have both in the past expressed strong views on Europe's economic integration -- said Germany should not enter a single currency at any cost.

And, with record unemployment still rated as Germany's number one economic problem, Bernhard Jagoda, the head of the country's jobs agency, warned that a union-proposed plan to cut working hours and create jobs simply would not work.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac, at a meeting late on Wednesday, reaffirmed their commitment to creating the single currency on time in 1999 and pledged to stick by the strict criteria for entry.

The leaders' political intentions were underscored by Finance Minister Theo Waigel and his deputy Juergen Stark, who stressed in speeches that Germany would rein in its budget deficit to achieve entry into economic and monetary union (EMU).

"Germany will fulfil the criteria," Waigel told a savings bank conference. "Even current developments give no cause to veer from these forecasts. But should there still be a need to act, we will not hesitate to do what is necessary."
Stark told a political meeting in Berlin that the economic criteria for EMU must be adhered to strictly.
"The criteria were not anchored in the Maastricht Treaty only for us then to depart from them. We want to take them seriously and we must take them seriously," he said.

Countries which wish to meld their currencies into the euro currency from 1999 must meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, public debt and budget deficits this year in advance of a 1998 decision on which nations will take part.

Germany, in common with several other European nations, is facing serious problems in reaching the public deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product. Its forecast for a deficit of 2.9 percent this year is deemed optimistic by many analysts.
Referring specifically to this requirement, Stark said, "We shall meet the deficit criterion. There is no doubt about that...I don't know where this doubt is coming from."

But a Portuguese newspaper delivered grounds for concern. El Publico said new European Commission forecasts for issue on April 23 showed Germany's deficit would hit 3.2 percent of GDP in 1997 -- the crunch year for EMU qualification.
A Commission spokesman declined to comment on their accuracy. "Work on the forecast is still continuing," he said.

Doubts about Germany's ability to meet the criteria also emanated from the Bundesbank council, as Reimut Jochimsen, who heads the regional central bank based in Dusseldorf, said it would be tough for Germany to fulfil the fiscal criteria.

"It is becoming increasingly evident that Germany will find it extraordinarily difficult to meet the budget and debt criteria," Jochimsen told a monthly magazine, adding that a delay in the launch of the euro currency could not be ruled out.
Speaking in Berlin, a second Bundesbank council member, Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, said problems in meeting the criteria meant the risk that the criteria would be interpreted too generously.
But he added: "...To me it is extremely questionable whether a postponement would lead to any improved (economic) convergence (between nations)."
Private sector economists said growth would have to accelerate further to reach 1997 targets but conditions were improving for this, even though risks related to sluggish domestic demand lingered.

Economists largely shared Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt's assessment on Wednesday that growth needed to speed up to reach Bonn's 2.5 percent goal but said fears Germany could fall far short of this goal should now be erased.
Gerhard Grebe, economist at Bank Julius Baer, commented, "The 2.5 percent rate is within reach".
But economists said this was not an excuse for Waigel to relax on reforms or on measures to rein in budget spending.
An extra percentage point of growth could subtract about 0.4 percentage points from the budget deficit compared to GDP, or add it in the reverse situation.

With this in mind, they said Waigel might opt to raise mineral oil tax to drum up another four to eight billion marks ($2.3 to $4.6 billion) for his coffers. He could also freeze spending again from mid-year.

In an indication that tax reform to help boost the competitiveness of German industry might be edging closer, Waigel said he was ready to reach a compromise with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) at talks which resume next week.
Talks on Waigel's package of 30 billion marks in income and corporate tax cuts are due to resume on Tuesday after Kohl agreed to an SPD demand that he take part in person. ($ = 1.722 German Marks)
